sentences.text: There was a night in October when the geese went over Szentmárton, and it was the only night of the year that anybody in that village stayed up on purpose.
They came late — never before eleven, usually nearer one — and they came low.
Lower than geese have any business flying.
Bori's father said you could hear the wingbeats, which she had assumed for years was an exaggeration, and then had heard them at nine years old and had never argued about it again.
It is a sound like a room full of people shaking out sheets, and it goes on for a long time, and it goes over the roofs at a height that makes the dogs mad.
You did not go out and watch.
That was the first rule and nobody had ever explained it and everybody kept it.
Bori had asked about that one more times than about anything else, and the answers were all versions of the same shrug.
Her father said you just didn't.
Her mother said it was rude.
The priest said, in a slightly evasive way, that it was a matter of respecting privacy, and did not specify whose.
The only answer that ever satisfied her came from old Feri at the workshop, who said: "Because you'd look." "That's the same thing." "No it's not.
You'd look, and you'd see whose is whose, and you'd see which windowsill's got one on it and which hasn't." He went back to the lathe.
"It's not the geese we're being polite to." You put your letter out before dark and you went in and you shut the door.
The letters were not letters in any sense a postman would recognise.

There was no envelope, no name, no address, and above all no signature — a signed one, said Bori's grandmother, is worse than useless, and the one time somebody had signed one in her lifetime the whole business had gone badly for a family that was no longer in the village to be embarrassed about it.
You wrote the thing you could not say.
That was the entire specification.
Not a wish.
Not a complaint.
Not a prayer, and the priest had been quite clear about that from the pulpit in 1988 and had privately put one out himself in 1991, which everybody knew and nobody mentioned.
The thing you could not say.
To the person you could not say it to.
In as many or as few words as it took.
Then you folded it once and put it somewhere outside — a windowsill, a fence post, the hollow in the wall by the chapel, wedged in a hedge — and you went indoors and did not look out.
In the morning they were gone.
Bori had tested this once, at ten, in a spirit of pure enquiry, and would like it recorded that she did not put out a real one to do it.
She wrote *this is not a real letter* on a piece of paper, folded it once, and put it on the sill.
It was there in the morning, damp and perfectly ordinary, and she took it in and felt obscurely told off.
Not blown about the lane, not soaked in the ditch, not caught in the fence.
Gone, all of them, every year, from a village of two hundred and six people in a country where the wind in October takes anything not nailed down.
